evidence_quotes.quote: Part 1 of this chapter describes the law and policy framework for the right to water in South Africa, where the constitutional right has been concretised in a number of legislative and policy documents including the Water Services Act (WSA), the National Water Act (NWA) and the Free Basic Water Policy.
In addition, the NWA de-links water rights and land ownership by replacing the previous riparian system of allocation, which linked water rights to land ownership, with a compulsory licensing regime

These provide that the minimum standard for basic water supply services subsumes inter alia a minimum quantity of potable water of twenty-five litres per person per day or six kilolitres per household per month, available within 200 metres of a household and with an effectiveness such that no consumer is without a supply for more than seven full days in any year.

evidence_quotes.criterion: effect_estimate and mechanism_flags (BURDEN: fees; ENFORCEMENT: disconnection)
evidence_quotes.quote: The other side of the coin is that accessibility of water services is contingent upon ability to pay. This has led in South Africa to rising use of water service disconnections, the installation of pre-paid water meters, and a certain level of privatisation of the water services sector.

evidence_quotes.criterion: mechanism_certainty and mechanism_flags (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: hardship_exception; ENFORCEMENT: disconnection)
evidence_quotes.quote: When the free 6 kilolitres of water is finished, the water supply is discontinued without any notice. There is no person to whom I can explain the reason why I cannot pay, or why I need the water to remain connected.

there remain persistent inequalities in the face of access to water services and infrastructure, and the implementation of the Government's Free Basic Water policy has met with serious obstacles in addressing problems of accessibility and affordability of water.

country.comment: Single-country legal and policy analysis of post-apartheid water governance and the right to water in South Africa, situated within international human rights law.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title & Introduction; PDF pp. 2-27

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative doctrinal and policy finding with no quantitative effect estimate. Cites secondary government figures from the 2003 Strategic Framework noting that in 2001, 11% of the population had no access to safe water supply, 15% lacked defined basic service levels, and 41% lacked adequate sanitation services (PDF p. 12, fn. 53).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Doctrinal and policy analysis finds that although South Africa entrenched a constitutional right of access to sufficient water (Section 27 of the 1996 Constitution), de-linked water rights from land ownership (1998 National Water Act), and guaranteed a Free Basic Water allocation of 6 kilolitres per household per month (25 litres per person per day for an 8-person household), concurrent full cost-recovery pricing, inadequate municipal funding/cross-subsidisation, corporatisation and privatisation, arrears disconnections, and pre-paid water meters have impeded affordable and continuous water access for poor households—automatically cutting off supply without notice or ability-to-pay review once the 6-kilolitre block is exhausted and forcing reliance on unsafe water sources.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 2, Introduction; PDF pp. 9-10, Section 1.C; PDF pp. 12-19, Sections 1.D & 2; PDF pp. 22-27, Section 4 & Concluding Remarks

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the non-experimental doctrinal-institutional design ceiling. Primary statutory and regulatory instruments together with sworn litigation filings cited on file with the author (Mazibuko Founding Affidavit, PDF p. 25, fn. 100) directly document how the flat 6 kL/month household threshold, cost-recovery tariffs, and automatic pre-paid meter cut-offs operate to terminate water access while bypassing notice, representation, and inability-to-pay protections under Section 4(3) of the Water Services Act.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 7-11, Sections 1.B-1.C; PDF pp. 13-19, Sections 1.D & 2; PDF pp. 22-26, Section 4

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines de-linking water rights from land ownership (property), municipal service jurisdiction duties (service_area), rising block tariffs, full cost-recovery charges, arrears, and upfront pre-payment (fees), state and municipal policy/tariff discretion (discretion), inability-to-pay protections under WSA Section 4(3)(c) and compassionate credit-control policies (hardship_exception), service cut-offs and automatic pre-paid meter disconnections (disconnection), constitutional reasonableness review and disconnection/pre-paid meter litigation (judicial_review), lack of public consultation and communication around corporatisation and pre-paid meter installation (participation), and national-local fiscal/mandate division alongside private-sector delegation (institutional_fragmentation).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, property, service_area, fees, discretion, hardship_exception, disconnection, judicial_review, participation, institutional_fragmentation
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 3-5, Section 1.A; PDF pp. 7-11, Sections 1.B-1.C; PDF pp. 13-26, Sections 1.D, 2, 3 & 4

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes physical and economic access to water and basic sanitation, minimum service quantity (25 L/person/day or 6 kL/household/month vs. 50-100 L/person/day), potable water quality standards and resort to polluted water sources, reliability of supply and faulty pre-paid meter devices, tariff affordability and household debt/arrears, service continuity/interruptions/cut-offs, and statutory restrictions on unreasonable refusal or denial of service.
